name: Chile
description: Chile offers expats a compelling blend of economic stability, diverse natural landscapes, and a high quality of life in South America. Its modern infrastructure and stable governance make it an attractive destination for those seeking a balance of urban amenities and outdoor adventure.
longdescription: Expat life in Chile is characterized by a high standard of living, particularly in major cities like Santiago, which boasts modern infrastructure, reliable communications, and efficient public transport. The country offers a diverse range of climates and environments, from the Atacama Desert to Patagonia, catering to various lifestyles. While the cost of living can be higher than in some neighboring South American countries, it is generally more affordable than many Western nations, especially concerning healthcare and services. Daily life is calm and family-centered, though new arrivals might find the culture more reserved and formal. Learning Chilean Spanish is highly recommended for integration, as English proficiency is not widespread outside business and tourist sectors. Safety in Chile is generally good compared to other Latin American nations, though petty crime like pickpocketing has seen an increase, particularly in crowded urban areas. The economy is stable, with opportunities in sectors like mining, renewable energy, and technology. Chile is an OECD member and has a well-developed network of free trade agreements, contributing to its economic strength.

Citizenship by Descent.desc: Chilean nationality law follows *jus sanguinis* (right of blood). Children born abroad to a Chilean father or mother are Chilean citizens from birth, as long as at least one parent held Chilean nationality at the time of the child's birth. This also extends to grandchildren if the intermediate parent was Chilean. There is typically a two-generation limit. No residency requirement in Chile is needed to claim citizenship by descent; the process involves registering the birth with the Chilean Civil Registry, often through a Chilean consulate.

Naturalization.desc: Permanent residents can apply for Chilean citizenship through naturalization. The standard requirement is 5 years of continuous legal residence in Chile, counted from the first temporary residency permit, with active permanent residency (Residencia Definitiva) at the time of application. Applicants must be at least 18 years old (14+ with parental consent), hold a clean criminal record, demonstrate financial stability, and show basic Spanish proficiency and knowledge of Chilean civic principles. The process can take 1 to 3 years after application. Chile allows dual citizenship.

Birthright.desc: Chile grants citizenship to almost all children born within its borders under the principle of *jus soli* (right of the soil). This applies regardless of the parents' residency status, meaning the child automatically becomes a Chilean citizen. Exceptions are rare, primarily for children of foreign diplomats or those of transient foreigners (tourists or transit passengers), who may instead opt for Chilean citizenship upon turning 18. Having a Chilean child can also simplify the residency path for foreign parents, allowing them to apply for a residence permit based on family ties and potentially apply for naturalization in a reduced timeframe (approximately 2-3 years after the child's birth).

Spouse and Family.desc: Marriage to a Chilean citizen does not automatically grant citizenship but provides an accelerated naturalization pathway. Spouses of Chilean citizens can apply for citizenship after 2 years of continuous residence in Chile, provided the marriage has been registered in Chile for at least two years and they have lived together during this period. Other direct family ties, such as parents, children, or siblings of Chilean citizens, or individuals adopted by Chilean citizens, may also qualify for the 2-year accelerated naturalization track. The application can only be filed from within Chile.

tax_advice:
*   **Tax Residency:** Individuals are considered tax residents if they are domiciled in Chile or present for more than 183 days within any 12-month period.
*   **Income Tax:** Residents are taxed on worldwide income at progressive rates from 0% to 40%. Non-residents are taxed only on Chilean-source income at a flat rate of 15% for professional/technical services and 35% for other income.
*   **Expat Tax Exemption:** New tax residents benefit from a three-year exemption on foreign-source income, meaning only Chilean-source income is taxed during this period. This can be extended for an additional three years upon request, offering up to six years of tax-free foreign income.
*   **Corporate Tax:** The general corporate income tax rate is 27%. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) can qualify for a reduced rate of 12.5% for tax years 2025-2027, reverting to 25% from 2029.
*   **VAT:** A Value-Added Tax (VAT) of 19% applies.
*   **Capital Gains Tax:** Generally taxable as ordinary income, with exceptions like a 10% tax for gains from selling shares with sufficient stock market presence. Non-residents face a 35% withholding tax on Chilean-source capital gains.
*   **Dual Taxation Treaties:** Chile has a comprehensive network of approximately 35 double taxation agreements, including a ratified treaty with the US as of early 2024, to prevent double taxation.
local_tips:
*   **Cost of Living:** A single person can expect to spend around $1,188 - $1,500 per month (excluding rent), while a family of four may need $2,500 - $2,850 per month. Rent for a one-bedroom apartment in a city center averages $487 - $680. Santiago is generally more expensive than regional cities.
*   **Language:** Spanish is essential for daily life and integration, especially outside major tourist and business areas. Chilean Spanish has distinct characteristics that can be challenging even for fluent speakers.
*   **Safety:** While Chile is one of the safest countries in Latin America, an increase in petty crime, pickpocketing, and phone snatching has been noted. Vigilance is advised, particularly in crowded areas. Safe neighborhoods in Santiago include Vitacura, Las Condes, Providencia, and Lo Barnechea.
*   **Registration:** Upon arrival, obtain your RUT (Rol Único Tributario), which is your Chilean tax and identification number, crucial for all official and financial transactions. Register with the Civil Registry for your Chilean ID card (Cédula de Identidad) within 30 days of your visa being activated.
*   **Healthcare:** Expats can enroll in either the public healthcare system (FONASA) or private health insurance (ISAPRE).
*   **Transportation:** Santiago has an extensive and modern public transportation system, including a metro and bus network.
